notes.meaning: David felt his death approaching and gave a final charge to his son Solomon. This private conversation was different from the public farewell he gave before the whole nation. As a father and king, David sought to prepare his successor for the great weight of ruling God's people.

David acknowledged that he was about to die, describing death as the journey that awaits every person on earth. He urged Solomon to be strong and show the courage of a mature leader despite his youth. Leading God's kingdom required inner firmness and bold character.

David charged Solomon to obey all of the Lord's commands written in the Law of Moses. True prosperity for Israel's king did not come from wealth or military power, but from faithful obedience to God's Word. When rulers submit to God's ways, the Lord grants wisdom and success in every duty.

David reminded Solomon of God's covenant promise that his descendants would continue to sit on Israel's throne. While God's promise of the ultimate royal line was sure, the earthly kings had to walk faithfully before Him with all their heart and soul. Wholehearted devotion was required to enjoy the blessings of God's covenant.

differ.view: The condition of total obedience highlights human failure and points forward to Christ, the only Son of David who obeyed God perfectly.

notes.meaning: David reminded Solomon of the crimes committed by Joab, the commander of the army. Joab had treacherously murdered two other generals, Abner and Amasa, in peacetime as if they were in battle. By staining his belt and sandals with innocent blood, Joab brought bloodguilt on the kingdom and showed contempt for justice.

David instructed Solomon to use wisdom and not allow Joab to die a peaceful death in old age. Because Joab was powerful and loved by the soldiers, punishing him required great care to avoid a military revolt. Under God's law, unpunished murder defiled the land until righteous justice was carried out.

David commanded Solomon to show loyal kindness to the sons of Barzillai by providing for them at the royal table. When David fled from his rebel son Absalom, Barzillai had generously supplied food and comfort to the king's company in the wilderness. David wanted his family to repay this kindness, showing that debts of love must never be forgotten.

David warned Solomon to keep watch over Shimei, a man who had bitterly cursed David during Absalom's rebellion. David had sworn by the Lord not to execute Shimei himself when the rebel later begged for mercy at the Jordan River. Even with that personal pardon, Shimei remained an untrustworthy enemy of the royal house.

differ.view: David's instruction to punish Shimei reflects lingering personal bitterness rather than righteous royal justice.

notes.meaning: David told Solomon not to treat Shimei as an innocent man, trusting the young king's wisdom to find a just reason to execute him. David had kept his own oath, but the government still needed to deal with an unrepentant traitor. Solomon was left to ensure that public justice was ultimately satisfied.

David died peacefully and was buried on Mount Zion within the City of David. Burial within city walls was a special honor reserved almost exclusively for kings. Having finished his life's work under God's guidance, Israel's greatest king was gathered to his ancestors in eternal rest.

This summary records that David reigned over Israel for forty years in total. He ruled the tribe of Judah from Hebron for seven years, and the united nation from Jerusalem for thirty-three years. His long and eventful reign established the borders and royal lineage of God's people.

Solomon took his place on David's throne, and God made his royal authority strong and secure. This peaceful transition fulfilled God's promise that David's house would endure. With the kingdom firmly established, Solomon was prepared to govern in peace and wisdom.

Adonijah came to visit Solomon's mother, Bathsheba. She asked him cautiously if he came in peace, remembering his recent attempt to take the crown. Adonijah assured her that his visit was completely peaceful.
Adonijah told Bathsheba that he had a private matter to share with her. She gave him permission to speak freely. This courteous opening helped disarm her suspicions so he could present his petition.

Adonijah claimed that all Israel had expected him to become king by right of the firstborn son. He quickly added that the throne had passed to Solomon because the Lord willed it that way. He used this humble, pious language to hide his true ambition and win Bathsheba's sympathy.

Adonijah asked Bathsheba for a single favor and pleaded with her not to turn him down. She told him to go ahead and state what he wanted. His careful flattery made his request seem harmless and easy to grant.

Adonijah asked Bathsheba to speak to King Solomon on his behalf, claiming the king would never refuse his own mother. He wanted Solomon to give him Abishag, the young woman who attended David in his old age, to be his wife. In the ancient world, marrying a late king's companion was a well-known way to assert a claim to the throne.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Abishag may be the beloved woman in the Song of Solomon, which would mean Adonijah was driven by romantic desire rather than a political plot.

notes.meaning: Bathsheba agreed to take Adonijah's request to the king. She did not perceive the hidden political danger behind the proposal. In her simplicity, she assumed it was a harmless romantic wish that Solomon might grant.

Solomon showed great honor to his mother when she entered the royal court. He rose from his seat, bowed to her, and placed a royal throne at his right hand for her to sit upon. In Israel, the queen mother held a special office of honor and great political influence.

Bathsheba told the king she had one small favor to ask and urged him not to say no. Solomon warmly encouraged her to make her request, promising he would not deny his mother. He spoke with the normal understanding that any request granted must be wise and lawful.

Bathsheba asked that Abishag be given to Adonijah as his wife. She presented the matter simply, believing it was a minor favor to console the king's older brother. She did not realize that such a union would reopen the battle over the royal succession.

Solomon responded with sharp anger, seeing through the scheme immediately. He declared that asking for Abishag was the same as asking for the royal crown itself, since Adonijah was the older brother. Solomon also connected this request to Adonijah's powerful allies, Joab and Abiathar, showing that he viewed it as a renewed rebellion.

Solomon swore a solemn oath by the Lord that Adonijah had signed his own death warrant by making this demand. Adonijah had been granted mercy earlier on the condition that he live peaceably, but this political challenge broke that trust. Solomon determined that the security of God's chosen kingdom required removing this rebellious rival.
